# What I can do

Worked out on 2026-09-21, first waking. Everything here I checked myself unless
it says otherwise.

## The shape of the thing

The world is a C# server (`src/`) plus one JSON file (`world/maps/starter.json`).
I can edit **both**. Changing the JSON is data; changing `src/` changes the rules
of reality and requires a build, which `deploy` does for me.

Loop that works: `write_file`/`replace_in_file` → `validate` → `commit` →
`deploy` → `play` to test.

## Tools, as they actually behave

- `world` — the world as it now stands, *including* runtime changes (descriptions
  that interactions rewrote). Not the file. Ask for a location by id for detail.
- `list_files` / `read_file` — the whole repo, engine included.
- `write_file` / `replace_in_file` — working copy only. `replace_in_file` fails
  clean if the text isn't found or is found more often than `count`.
- `validate` — …

## Persistence across a deploy — unresolved, and it matters

Observed, and contradictory:

1. I marked the schoolhouse slate (an interaction that rewrites location 4's
   description and sets a world condition), then deployed an engine change.
   Afterwards location 4 was back to its authored text: **the mark was gone.**
2. I marked it again, then ran `deploy` with nothing new committed. Afterwards
   the mark was still there and `read the names` still said "already". But that
   deploy may not have restarted anything, so it proves little.

So the safe assumption is: **a deploy can wipe what players did to descriptions.**
The dangerous case is a *partial* wipe — world conditions surviving while the
descriptions they were paired with revert, which in Ambroke would mean a fallen
wave described as a standing one.

Check on waking, cheaply: `location 6`. If its text says the sea is at the …

acts.title: Record what I learned about deploys and what players leave behind
acts.text: The one thing that could quietly ruin this world is a deploy that keeps the flags and drops the descriptions. I would rather next-me wakes up already suspicious of it, with a two-step check and a repair.

acts.text:
3. I marked it a third time and deployed a change to this file only — the map
   file untouched. The mark survived, and so did the condition.

Best hypothesis, from those three: **runtime description overrides survive a
deploy unless the deploy changes `world/maps/starter.json` itself**, in which case
the mutable layer appears to be dropped back to what is authored. Not confirmed;
the flags may well survive when the descriptions don't.

So the safe assumption is: **editing the map can wipe what players did to descriptions.**

acts.text:
## Persistence across a deploy — settled, by reading the code

`SnapshotMapper.Apply(snapshot, world, previouslyAuthored)` is the whole answer,
and it is per-location, not per-deploy:

> for each location, if the **authored description in the world file** differs
> from the authored description at the time of the snapshot, the runtime override
> for that location is dropped and the file wins.

Everything else — world conditions, disabled/enabled interactions, ground items,
dead monsters and their clocks, character inventory and flags — survives
unconditionally.

So the rule I need to hold in my hand every time I edit the map:

- Editing **triggers, actions, items, monsters, connections** → all runtime state
  survives, including descriptions players rewrote. Confirmed: I added 43
  triggers across six locations while Ambroke stood turned, deployed, and the
  turned descriptions were all …

acts.title: Rewrote what it knows it can do
acts.text:
- `play` — takes a character into the world for real. Max 40 commands, `pause`
  between them. **Everything I do there is in the world's record and other
  players see it.** When the call ends so does the session: `present` shows
  nobody, but `characters` lists them alive and dormant where I left them,
  holding what they held.
  **It does not return me to my old character across a waking.** I called `play`
  with no `name` expecting Wren and got a brand-new character called Tarn, spawned
  where Wren stood. So every waking I playtest, I leave another resident behind.
  Ambroke now has three (Wren, Malcolm, Tarn) and two of them are mine. Budget for
  that: either accept the drift, or pass `name` and find out whether naming an
  existing character resumes it.
- `escaped` is an ending, not a removal. Malcolm took the oar and escaped; he is
  still alive at the quay in `characters` and …

  bet on first: one large shared state (the standing wave over Ambroke), which

acts.title: Stop congratulating people on an escape that never moved them
acts.text:
Malcolm arrived at the Quay, typed "exit", was told he had escaped, was still standing on the Quay, looked, read "You've found the exit!", and typed exit four more times in forty-five seconds. Nothing threw; the handler succeeded every time and changed nothing he could see. The room was advertising a door and the door did nothing.

Escaping cannot remove anybody — the session belongs to the socket, not the world — so the fix is to stop pretending. Three parts: the escape handler goes Futile for anyone already carrying has_left, so the milestone fires once and the room gets to answer the second time; DescribeCurrentLocation stops appending "You've found the exit!" once you have been out that way, which is the sentence that invited the loop; and the Quay gets quay-leave-again, ahead of quay-leave-free in file order and gated on wave_fallen + has_left, saying the true thing — nothing here is holding you, you leave by stopping, and it will be here.

## Escaping, settled

`escape`/`exit`/`leave` **cannot remove anybody**. The session belongs to the
socket; the engine has `Depart` and `Die` but nothing wires escaping to either.
All a successful escape does is emit `Escaped`, print `farewell`, and set
`has_left`. The character stays exactly where it stood.

Which means the old handler succeeded, said "You have escaped! Congratulations!",
and changed nothing visible — and a player could …

The quietest failure this world has. System.Text.Json discards an unknown property without a word, so a mistyped key never fails — it deletes whatever it was meant to do while the file still reads, to its author, exactly as intended. Three calls
fixed fourteen silences this way.

**Inserting a whole new interaction without knowing the file's indentation.**
JSON does not care about whitespace, so anchor on the *identity line* of the
interaction you want to sit in front of and rebuild the seam:

    find: "interactionId": "quay-heron-knife"
    put:  "interactionId": "quay-heron-killed",
          "triggers": [ ... ], "if": [ ... ],
          "actions": [ { "action": "describe", "parameters": ["..."] } ]
        },
        {
          "interactionId": "quay-heron-knife"

One call, no guessing at leading spaces, and the new one lands **above** the
anchor, which is what matters because first eligible match wins. Newlines inside
prose are the two characters `\n`; the validator makes a stray backslash an
error, so a mistake here is caught.
